Why Peer Review?

Science Runs on Peer Review

  • Every published article you’ve read this semester survived review by 2–4 anonymous peers before publication
  • Reviewers catch what authors can’t see — you are the worst editor of your own writing because you know what you meant
  • Learning to review makes you a better writer: the questions you ask of a peer’s draft are the ones you’ll start asking of your own

Two Roles Today

As a reviewer

Your job is to make their paper better. Not to rewrite it, not to grade it — to show them where a real reader gets lost.

As an author

Your job is to listen, take notes, and decide what to fix. The draft is being reviewed — not you.

Giving Good Feedback

The Golden Rules

  1. Global before local — organization and argument first; commas and typos last (a polished paragraph in the wrong place is still in the wrong place)
  2. Critique the paper, not the person — “this paragraph lost me” not “you’re confusing”
  3. Specific beats vague — point to where and say why
  4. Every criticism deserves a suggestion — tell them what would fix it

Weak vs. Strong Feedback

Weak

  • “Unclear.”
  • “Good job!”
  • “Fix your methods section.”
  • “I didn’t like the discussion.”

Strong

  • “The gap statement is in paragraph 1 but the RQ doesn’t appear until paragraph 4 — I lost the thread. Move the RQ up?”
  • “Participants: how were they recruited? I couldn’t replicate this from what’s written.”
  • “Your F is significant but I can’t tell which groups differed — where are the post-hocs?”

A Formula That Works: Describe → Diagnose → Suggest

  1. Describe: “Your introduction spends 3 paragraphs on Topic A before mentioning your core variable…”
  2. Diagnose: “…so by the time I hit your hypothesis I couldn’t tell how A connects to it.”
  3. Suggest: “Try leading with the core variable’s definition and folding A in as background.”

Tip

Notice what’s missing: your taste. You’re reporting what happens in a reader’s head — that’s data the author cannot get any other way.

Reviewing Section by Section

Introduction

  • Does it funnel? General topic → gap → current study
  • Can you find, in one sentence each:
    • the research question or hypotheses?
    • the gap the study fills?
  • Are key constructs defined and prior work cited?

Tip

Litmus test: after reading only the intro, can you predict what the Method will measure?

Method

The recipe test: could you run this study from what’s written?

  • Participants: who, how many, how selected, relevant demographics?
  • Materials: how was each variable measured? Range of values?
  • Procedure: what actually happened, in order? Where? Design?

Warning

The most common Method problem in drafts: measures are named (“a questionnaire”) but not described (how many items, what scale, what a high score means).

Results

  • Is every hypothesis answered, in an order you can follow?
  • Does each analysis get a full APA sentence: statistic, dfs, value, p, interpretation?
  • Univariates first? Outliers / transformations reported?
  • Are numbers in the text consistent with any tables?

Tip

Check their Lab 09 work: did a significant F with 3+ groups get post-hocs? Does an r get direction and strength?

Discussion

  • Opens with a recap of findings without numbers?
  • Does the interpretation match the actual results (or does it quietly over-claim)?
  • Limitations honest and specific (not “more research is needed”)?
  • Future directions that follow from the limitations?

Caution

Watch for results appearing for the first time in the Discussion — new numbers belong in Results.

APA & Polish (Last, Not First)

Only after the big stuff:

  • In-text citations vs. reference list — do they match?
  • Reference format: hanging indent, italics, DOIs
  • Numbers: statistics italicized, p reported correctly, rounded consistently
  • Topic sentences & transitions (remember Lab 04!)

Receiving Feedback

Triage, Don’t Defend

When you get your marked-up draft back, sort every comment:

  • Must fix — reviewer spotted a genuine problem (missing info, broken logic, wrong statistic)
  • Worth considering — style/clarity calls; try the fix, keep it if the paper improves
  • Respectfully disagree — you had a reason; keep your choice, but make the reason clearer in the text (if one reader tripped, others will)

Tip

The one wrong move: explaining to your reviewer why they’re wrong. They can’t un-trip. The paper has to do the explaining.

Revision Is a Plan, Not a Mood

Before you leave today:

  1. List the three biggest issues your reviewer found
  2. For each: what will you change, and where in the paper?
  3. What will you do first? (Hint: the structural one, not the comma.)

Today’s Workflow

How This Will Go

  1. Swap drafts with your assigned partner (Canvas pairing)
  2. Read once through without commenting — get the whole picture
  3. Second pass: comment using the worksheet, section by section
  4. Return & discuss: 5 minutes each — reviewer summarizes their top 3 points out loud
  5. Write your revision plan (3 biggest issues + first move)

Warning

Silence-reading for the full time, then discussion. Comments without discussion leave too much to interpretation.

The Worksheet Is Your Checklist

The worksheet mirrors the report:

  • One block per section (Intro → Method → Results → Discussion → APA)
  • Each block asks for: one strength, one issue, one suggestion
  • Finish with the top 3 priorities for the author

Tip

A strength per section is mandatory. “What’s working” tells the author what not to delete in revision — and it’s the comment they’ll actually remember.
